description_ru: Тридцать лет актёр ждёт в кулисах, пока главная звезда заболеет. Ироничная и грустная история о терпении, тщеславии и одной-единственной ночи.
text:
For thirty-one years, Desmond Quill had been the best-prepared man in the Marlowe Theatre, and for thirty-one years nobody had noticed, which is the peculiar fate of the understudy. He knew every line of every leading role in the repertoire. He knew where the great Augustin Vane liked to pause, where he coughed, where he forgot his lines and improvised a Latin tag that the critics, with touching loyalty, took for Shakespeare. Desmond knew all of it, and he kept it in the drawer of his mind like a spare key to a house he was never invited to enter.

His routine was almost monastic. Each evening he arrived an hour before the curtain, hung his good suit in a cupboard that smelled faintly of mothballs and despair, and took his place in the wings on a three-legged stool that had been there since the Coronation. From that vantage he mouthed the words in silence, a ghost haunting a performance that was not yet dead. The stage manager, a brisk woman named Philippa, referred to him as "the insurance", with the cheerful brutality of someone who has never had to be insured against.

Augustin Vane, meanwhile, was a man of splendid and indestructible health. He had survived two marriages, a bout of pneumonia in Manchester, and a chandelier that fell in 1987 and missed him by the width of a toupee. He greeted Desmond every night with the same blessing: "Still here, old boy? Marvellous. Do keep it warm." And Desmond, who had long ago perfected the art of smiling with the lower half of his face only, would answer that he was doing his humble best.

There had been moments of temptation, naturally. In the third decade, a young director had hinted that Vane was beginning to sound like a man reading his own obituary aloud, and Desmond had felt a small, shameful flutter, as of a bird in a locked room. He had gone straight home and made a cup of tea so strong it could have propped up a bridge. Hope, he had concluded, was a form of rudeness, and he had no wish to be rude to a colleague who had once lent him an umbrella.

Then, on a drizzling Thursday in November, the impossible occurred. Vane, mid-sentence in the fourth act, put his hand to his chest, regarded the audience with an expression of mild astonishment, and sat down heavily on the royal throne, which creaked in protest. It was only a dizzy spell, as the doctors later explained, brought on by an overly ambitious pastry at lunch. But the curtain came down, a hush fell over the house, and Philippa appeared in the wings with a face like a general who has misplaced a war.

"Desmond," she said. "You're on."

He rose from the stool. His knees, which had been rehearsing their own small rebellion for years, announced themselves like a pair of arthritic trumpets. He crossed to the costume rail, where the great king's robe hung in its velvet majesty, and slid it over his shoulders. It was three sizes too large. It smelled of Vane's cologne, a heady mixture of sandalwood and self-regard. He stood for a moment in the half-dark, aware that the whole building was listening, and he felt, absurdly, not terror but a kind of vast and tender calm, the sort one feels on finally being asked a question one has answered in the bath for thirty years.

The curtain rose. The audience, informed by a nervous announcement that Mr. Vane was indisposed, shifted in their seats with the weary resignation of people who have paid for champagne and been served tap water. Desmond walked to the centre of the stage and began.

What followed, according to those who were there, could not be described as acting. It was something more like a long-delayed arrival. He did not pause where Vane paused; he found, instead, silences that nobody had known the play contained. When he spoke the great speech about the weight of the crown, the theatre went so quiet that one could hear the radiators ticking, and a woman in the stalls, who had come only to be seen in a new hat, forgot entirely about her hat. He was not a better actor than Vane, perhaps. He was merely a man who had waited so long, and listened so carefully, that every word arrived in his mouth already ripened.

At the final curtain there was a pause so long that Desmond assumed, with that old reflex of apology, that he had somehow ruined everything. Then the applause broke over him like surf. People stood. Somebody shouted his name, which was a shock, since he had not been aware that anybody knew it. Philippa, in the wings, was crying quietly into a clipboard.

In the morning the newspapers were uncharacteristically unanimous. One called him "a revelation that had been hiding in plain sight for three decades"; another, more waspish, wondered how a theatre could manage to mislay such talent for so long, and suggested the management be examined for carelessness. Augustin Vane, recovering in a private room with a bunch of grapes the size of grenades, read the reviews twice, set them down with great care, and said to his wife, "Well. That is inconvenient."

By Saturday he was back on stage, because the public, for all its sentimentality, still bought tickets for the name above the title, and Desmond returned to his three-legged stool. Nothing, in the strict accounting of the world, had changed. The tradition of the theatre is that the understudy gets one night, and then the star resumes his rightful place, with a graciousness that costs him nothing and an irritation that costs him everything.

Yet something had shifted in the wings. The stagehands, who had once passed Desmond with a nod, now stopped to shake his hand. Philippa stopped calling him the insurance. And Vane, that evening, paused at the stool, cleared his throat, and said, with the stiff reluctance of a man handing over a very small coin, "You were rather good, you know."

"Thank you," said Desmond. "I had a good teacher."

It was not flattery, and it was not irony either, or not entirely. He had, after all, learned every inflection from the man. But as the king stalked on stage to a ripple of applause, Desmond settled onto his stool, folded his hands, and mouthed the first line of the next scene, and he noticed, with quiet astonishment, that the key in the drawer of his mind had begun, very faintly, to fit a lock.

Кончик языка между зубами, звук звонкий. Не заменяйте на з или д.

questions.question: How long had Desmond Quill been an understudy?
Why did Augustin Vane stop in the fourth act?
questions.answer: He felt dizzy, brought on by a pastry at lunch.

questions.question: How did the critics react to Desmond's performance?
questions.answer: They were unanimous in praising him as a revelation.

questions.question: What did Vane say to Desmond afterwards?
questions.answer: That he had been rather good.
